coredata.dc:description: A polylactic acid degrading triacylglycerol lipase (TGL) was identified from Bacillus safensis based on genome annotation and validated by real-time quantitative PCR. TGL displayed optimal activity at pH 9.0 and 55 °C. It maintained stability at pH 9.0 and temperatures 45 °C. The activity of TGL was found to benefit from the presence of potassium sodium ions, and low concentrations of Triton X-100. The TGL could erode the surface of polylactic acid films and increase its hydrophilicity. The hydrolysis products of polylactic acid by TGL were lactate monomer and dimer. TGL contains a classical catalytic triad structure of lipase (Ser77, Asp133, and His156) and an Ala-X-Ser-X-Gly sequence. Compared with some lipases produced by the same genus Bacillus, TGL is highly conserved in its amino acid sequence, mainly reflected in the amino acid residues that exercise the enzyme activity, including the catalytic activity center and the substrate binding sites.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A polylactic acid degrading triacylglycerol lipase (TGL) was identified from Bacillus safensis based on genome annotation and validated by real-time quantitative PCR. TGL displayed optimal activity at pH 9.0 and 55 °C. It maintained stability at pH 9.0 and temperatures 45 °C. The activity of TGL was found to benefit from the presence of potassium sodium ions, and low concentrations of Triton X-100. The TGL could erode the surface of polylactic acid films and increase its hydrophilicity. The hydrolysis products of polylactic acid by TGL were lactate monomer and dimer. TGL contains a classical catalytic triad structure of lipase (Ser77, Asp133, and His156) and an Ala-X-Ser-X-Gly sequence. Compared with some lipases produced by the same genus Bacillus, TGL is highly conserved in its amino acid sequence, mainly reflected in the amino acid residues that exercise the enzyme activity, including the catalytic activity center and the substrate binding sites.

ce:section.ce:para: The environmental pollution caused by plastic waste has become increasingly serious with the development of the plastic industry and the widespread use of disposable plastic products [1]. The application of degradable plastics was considered a potential solution to the environmental pollution caused by petroleum-derived non-biodegradable plastics [2]. The common biodegradable plastics mainly include polylactic acid (PLA), poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), poly (butylene succinate) (PBS), polycaprolactone (PCL) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA). PLA, owing to its excellent mechanical and thermal properties is widely used [3]. PLA, a linear aliphatic polyester, is formed by linking lactic acid monomers through ester bonds. The degradation of PLA primarily involves the cleavage of the main or side chains of the macromolecule. Specifically, the hydrolysis of the ester group leads to the release of lactic acid molecules, causing a reduction in PLA polymerization. Additionally, intramolecular random protonation of ester-based carbon facilitates ester bond hydrolysis, generating various lower molecular weight fragments [4]. Although biodegradable, PLA tends to degrade very slowly in the natural environment. For instance, it neither degraded after 428 days in the marine environment [5], nor did it biodegrade under anaerobic biological conditions in a mesophilic landfill [6]. This could be due to the limited distribution of species and less abundance of microorganisms that can degrade PLA in the environment [7].

Some microorganisms belonging to Bacillus exhibit the capability to degrade PLA. For instance, complete degradation of PLA films was achieved by B. pumilus within a 2-week co-culture [8]. In another study, co-incubation with B. smithii for 3 days resulted in a 35.6 % reduction in the molecular weight of PLLA [9]. Additionally, B. licheniformis was found to cause a 60 % loss in the weight of pure PLA after 5 months of co-incubation [10]. The genome analysis of B. altitudinis led to the identification of a PLA depolymerase with the capacity to degrade high molecular weight PLA. Interestingly, there exists an amino acid sequence similarity between the PLA depolymerase and the PBAT-degrading enzyme produced by B. pumilus [11].

Biodegradation of polymers, including PLA, is achieved through the action of appropriate degrading enzymes secreted by microorganisms. The majority of the PLA-degrading enzymes produced by fungi and actinomycetes belong to the families of proteases and cutinases [12–15], whereas the PLA-degrading enzymes produced by bacteria are likely to be lipases [16], cutinases [17], esterases [10] and proteases [18]. Akutsu-Shigeno et al. reported a lipase obtained from Paenibacillus amylolyticus that could degrade PLA to lactate monomer [19]. Masaki et al. isolated the PLA-degrading cutinase Cle from Cryptococcus sp. S-2, which could completely degrade high molecular weight pure PLA within 6 h at a concentration of 0.8 μg/mL [17]. Hazrat et al. found an esterase from Pseudomonas aeruginosa S3 exhibiting high hydrolase activity against PLA at 30 °C [20]. Mahbod et al. screened two esterases (ABO2449 and RPA1511) with the ability to degrade PLA. The lactate monomers and oligomers were also detected in the hydrolyzed products of PLA [21].

In our previous study, a mesophilic bacteria B. safensis PLA1006, with degradability towards PLA, had been identified from the soils collected from landfills [22]. In this work, the PLA-degrading enzyme was further identified from B. safensis PLA1006 by sequencing the whole genome and annotation combined with real-time quantitative PCR (RT q-PCR) validation. Following the clonal expression and purification of PLA-degrading enzymes, the enzymatic properties and PLA degrading ability of the enzyme were investigated.

PLA (Revode 101) with a weight-average molar mass (Mw) of 135,000 was supplied by Zhejiang HISUN Biological Material Co., LTD (HISUN, Taizhou, China). B. safensis PLA 1006 was previously isolated from landfill soil [22]. The MSM medium contained (per liter): 4.54 g KH2PO4, 11.94 g Na2HPO4·H2O, 1.0 g NH4Cl, 0.5 g MgSO4, 5 mg CaCl2, 2 mg FeSO4, 1 mg MnSO4, and 2 mg ZnSO4, pH 7.0 [23]. The PLA emulsion was prepared according to previous reports with some modifications [24]. PLA particles (2 g) were dissolved in 20 mL of dichloromethane. Subsequently, this solution was emulsified by sonication (50 W, 10 min) in 400 mL of MSM using 0.01 % (w/v) Plysurf A210G (Daiichi Kougyou Seiyaku, Tokyo, Japan) as an emulsifier. The resulting emulsion was subjected to heating at 80 °C with stirring for 2 h to eliminate dichloromethane, resulting in the formation of the PLA emulsion.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Genome extraction and sequencing of B. safensis PLA1006
ce:section.ce:para: A single colony of B. safensis PLA1006 was inoculated in Luria–Bertani (LB) nutrient broth and cultured overnight at 30 °C with shaking (150 rpm). The whole genome was extracted using SteadyPure Bacterial Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (Accurate Biology, Changsha, China). The DNA samples were randomly interrupted for 10s on/10s off/30 cycles using the Ultrasonic crushing apparatus (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA). A VAHTS Universal Plus DNA Library Prep Kit for MGI V2 (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was used to prepare the whole DNA library (including end repair, A-tail addition, sequencing ligation addition, purification, and PCR amplification). The PCR amplification conditions were as follows: 1 cycle of 3 min at 94 °C, 6 cycles each of 20 s at 98 °C, 15 s at 60 °C, and 30 s at 72 °C.

Following the library construction, initial quantification was performed using a Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Subsequently, the library was diluted and the inserts were detected using a Bioanalyzer 2100 system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Once the insert sizes were as expected, the effective concentration (50 ng·μL−1) of the library was accurately quantified using real-time fluorescence quantitative PCR instrument C1000 Touch (BioRad, Hercules, CA, USA). The libraries that passed the test were pooled into flow cells according to the effective concentration and the target offline data volume. Clonal clusters were generated using the cBot 2 Cluster Generation System (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA), and sequencing was performed using the Illumina high-throughput sequencing platform NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA).

The obtained raw reads were filtered using FastQC version 0.11.9 and Sickle version 1.33. The high-quality adapter-free filtered reads were assembled using SPAdes version 3.9.0 and polished by Pilon [25]. Genome assembly was performed based on the method of Wick et.al [26] and the genomic framework of B. safensis F6 (CP043404.1) [27]. Gene prediction procedures including signal peptide prediction [28], genomic island prediction [29], cytochrome P450 protein family prediction [30], ARDB-antibiotic resistance gene prediction [31], and membrane transporter protein prediction [32] were performed. A circular map of the strain PLA 1006 genome was generated using CG viewer [33].

PLA1006 strain was inoculated into two different media: MSMG (MSM with a final concentration of 2.5 mg·mL−1 glucose) and MSMP medium (MSM with a final concentration of 2.5 mg·mL−1 PLA) and were incubated at 30 °C for 5 days. The microbial colonies were collected at the end of the culture after washing with sterile saline, and an equal number of cells were used for RNA extraction after measuring the absorbance at 600 nm. Total RNA was extracted using the Bacteria Total RNA Isolation Kit (Sangon, Shanghai, China) and cDNA reverse transcription was performed using the M-MuLV First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Sangon, Shanghai, China). The ability of microorganisms to degrade polyesters is due to the secretion of enzymes specialized in polyester degradation, including proteases, lipases, esterases, cutinases, and α/β-hydrolases, in the extracellular environment. Therefore, genes encoding these enzymes with signal peptides were selected as candidate genes within the genome and the corresponding primers were designed (Fig. S1). The expression levels of the genes were determined by RT q-PCR using ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) [34].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning and expression of PLA-degrading enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: The selected PLA degrading enzyme gene was subcloned in the pET-28a(+) vector through PCR amplification. The 3′-primer with BamHI digestion site was CGCG^GATCCGCTGAGCATA ATCCGGTTGTG, and the 5′-primer with XhoI digestion site was CCGC^TCGAGCGTA TTCTGTCCTCCGCCGTTC. The PCR conditions were as follows: 1 cycle of 5 min at 94 °C, 30 cycles each of 45 s at 94 °C, 30 s at 55 °C, and 1 min at 72 °C. PCR products and vectors were digested with BamHI and XhoI, and then purified with General DNA Product Purification Kits (Tiangen, Beijing, China) and ligated using T4 DNA Ligase (Sangon, Shanghai, China). The recombinant plasmid was transferred into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. The cells were plated on LB agar-supplemented kanamycin with a final concentration of 50 μg·mL−1, and incubated at 37 °C overnight [35].

Positive clones were inoculated into 600 mL LB medium and incubated at 37 °C with shaking (180 rpm) until OD600 reached 0.6–0.8. IPTG was added to the medium with a final concentration of 0.2 mM, and the incubation was continued for 18 h at 18 °C with shaking [36]. After incubation, the bacterial precipitate was collected by centrifugation (8,000 rpm, 10 min) and resuspended in binding buffer (20 mM phosphate buffer, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). Subsequently, the suspension was subjected to sonication (2 s on/4 s off/20 min) in an ice bath and then centrifuged (12,000 rpm, 10 min). The supernatant was collected as supernatant crude protein and the precipitate was dissolved in a binding buffer containing 6 M urea to yield precipitate crude protein. Subsequently, the crude protein sample was combined with His-tag Protein Purification beads (BeaverBeads, Suzhou, China) in a centrifuge tube and rotated for 30 min at room temperature using a rotary mixer. The mixture was then subjected to magnetic separation using a magnetic separator, followed by removal of the supernatant. The beads were washed twice with washing buffer (20 mM phosphate buffer, 500 mM NaCl, 50 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). After washing, elution buffer (20 mM phosphate buffer, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 7.4) was added to the centrifuge tube. Gentle agitation ensured bead suspension, followed by magnetic separation. Then the eluent containing the purified protein sample was collected. Protein concentrations of whole cells, supernatants, precipitates, and purified enzymes were assayed using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The supernatant, precipitate and purified samples were collected for subsequent SDS-PAGE and Western blotting, respectively. The samples were separated on 12 % BeyoGel™ SDS-PAGE Precast Gel(Beyotime, Shanghai, China) and transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked with 2 % skim milk in PBST before overnight incubation with His-Tag Mouse Monoclonal Antibody(Beyotime, Shanghai, China) in PBST(1:500, v/v). The blots were incubated with HRP-labeled Goat Anti-Mouse Antibody (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) in PBST for 1 h. Membranes were developed with Chemistar™ High-sig ECL Western Blotting Substrate (Tanon, Shanghai, China) and detected using ChemiDoc™ XRS+ Imaging System (BioRad, Hercules, CA, USA).

The lipase activity assay was conducted following the previously reported method with slight modifications [37,38]. A 1 mmol nitrophenol palmitate (p-NPP) solution was prepared by completely dissolving 37.7 mg of p-NPP in 10 mL isopropanol. This solution was then added to 20 mM pH 7.0 PBS buffer, which served as the substrate for the lipase activity assay. The enzyme sample and substrate were mixed in a ratio of 1:9. The enzyme sample and substrate were mixed in a ratio of 1:9. Following incubation at 37 °C for 10 min, the absorbance of the mixture at 410 nm was measured. PBS buffer with 10 % isopropanol was used as a negative control to avoid interference from the self-hydrolysis of the substrate. Enzyme activity unit (U) was defined as the amount of 1 μmol of p-nitrophenol produced per min. Specific activities were expressed as U per mg protein per min.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of temperature, pH, metal ions, and chemicals on recombinant enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: The enzyme and p-NPP substrates were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min in different buffer solutions of varying pH (pH 4.0–6.0, 20 mM acetate buffer; pH 6.0–8.0, 20 mM phosphate buffer; pH 8.0–10.0; 20 mM Tris-HCl buffer) to determine the optimal pH. Similarly, the optimal temperature was obtained by incubating the enzyme and p-NPP substrates at different temperatures (25–70 °C) for 10 min at optimized pH. For the assessment of pH stability, the enzyme was pre-incubated in 20 mM Tris-HCl buffers with different pH (pH 8.0, 9.0 and10.0) at optimized temperature and determine the enzyme activity every 6 h within 24 h. To assess thermostability, the purified enzyme in 20 mM Tris-HCl buffers (pH 9.0) was kept at different temperatures (45, 50, 55 and 60 °C) for 24 h and the enzyme activity was determined every 6 h. The effects of metal ions and chemicals on enzyme activity were determined by incubating the enzyme with p-NPP substrate containing metal ions (1 mM and 10 mM) and chemicals (1 % and 5 %). Specific activities were tested under standard conditions and the results were also expressed as relative enzyme activity. The standard conditions are described in Section 2.6. The enzyme activity obtained under standard conditions was considered 100 % activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Enzyme kinetics and substrate specificity analysis
ce:section.ce:para: The parameters for enzyme kinetics were determined by measuring the production of p-NP in 20 mM Tris-HCl buffer (20 mM, pH 9.0) containing p-NPP and other substrates with side chain lengths ranging from C2-C18, at 55 °C for 10 min [39].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Biodegradation of PLA emulsion and films by purified recombinant enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: The absorbance at 630 nm was recorded by adding 0.5 mL of 100 μg/mL purified recombinant enzymes (about 17.5 U) to 1.5 mL PLA emulsion at 55 °C for 12 h. The control was 0.5 mL of Tris-HCl buffer (pH 9.0) added to 1.5 mL PLA emulsion. The hydrolytic ability of the recombinant enzymes was evaluated by comparing the turbidity changes in the PLA emulsions with the control.

PLA films (10 mm × 10 mm × 0.3 mm) were immersed in 1 mL Tris-HCl buffer (20 mM, pH 9.0) containing 100 μg·mL−1 recombinant enzyme (about 35 U) and incubated with shaking (60 rpm) at 55 °C for 12 h. The weight of the film was recorded after periodic sampling (every 2 h), cleaning, and drying. The weight loss and degradation rate of PLA films were calculated according to Eq. (1) and Eq. (2).

The surface morphology, microstructure, and hydrophilic properties of the degraded PLA films were studied using Hitachi SU8010 scanning electron microscope (SEM, Tokyo, Japan) and Kruss DSA100 (Hamburg, Germany) water contact angles measurement (WCA), respectively. The PLA films were cleaned before analysis and the film surfaces were sputtered with gold for SEM analysis. The WCA was measured five times under static conditions at room temperature. The degradation products of PLA in the PBS buffer were detected using Applied Bio-systems 4700 Proteomics Analyzer matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The conditions for analysis were as follows; capillary voltage was 3.5 kV, tapered hole voltage was 20 kV, RF lens voltage was 0.5 V, and source temperature was 120 °C [22].

ce:section.ce:section-title: 3D structural model prediction and molecular docking
ce:section.ce:para: The amino acid sequence of PLA degrading enzyme from B. safensis and similar sequences of triacylglycerol lipases from other Bacillus species were obtained from the NCBI protein database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/). The 3D model of PLA degrading enzyme from PLA1006 was constructed using the SWISS-MODEL automated modeling program (https://swissmodel.expasy.org). Alignment of the amino acid sequences for PLA degradation enzymes and similar sequences derived from other Bacillus species was performed by the END script server. (https://espript.ibcp.fr/ESPript/) [40].

Schrödinger's software was used for preprocessing of target protein crystal structure, regenerate states of native ligands, H-bond assignment optimization, protein energy minimization, and removal of water. The substrate for docking, lactate dimer, was processed using the LigPrep module in Schrödinger software, and all its 3D chiral conformations were generated. Molecular docking of lactate dimer to the active site of the target protein was carried out using the glide module (the highest precision XP docking). The docking coordinates were X = 26.62, Y = 40.48, Z = 7.58, and the range of x, y, and z were 10 Å. The binding ability of the lactate dimer to the active site of the target protein was analyzed by MM-GBSA calculations, and the MM-GBSA dG Bind served as an approximation for the binding free energy profile of the ligand to the protein. Finally, the results were post-processed with Maestro 13.5 to demonstrate the molecule-protein interaction patterns. The bond length and bond energy were analyzed according to the website (https://plip-tool.biotec.tu-dresden.de/).

All experiments were performed in triplicate. The statistical analysis was carried out using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Duncan's multiple range test (DMRT) or Student's t-test in SPSS 26 software. The values are presented as means ± SD and the results were considered as statistically significant at p < 0.05 or p < 0.01.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Genome annotation analysis of B. safensis PLA1006
ce:section.ce:para: Genome sequencing of B. safensis PLA 1006 was performed using the Oxford Nanopore and Illumina platforms. The gene functions were annotated using eight databases, namely, UniProt, Pfam, Refseq, Non-redundant (NR), Tigrfam, Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes, and Genomes (KEGG), and Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COG). The whole-genome sequences are available in GenBank (accession numbers CP114177.1). The results (Fig. 1a) showed that the whole genome of PLA1006 included 3,891,304 base pairs (bp). The predicted coding genes and nucleotide count of coding genes were 3965 and 3,481,120 bp, respectively. The genome of B. subtilis Bbv57 encompassed 4,302,465 bp, including 4363 coding genes [41], whereas the genome of B. licheniformis DSM13 comprised 4,222,748 bp and covered 4286 coding genes [42]. PLA1006 contained a smaller genome and fewer genes as compared to B. subtilis and B. licheniformis. The whole genome functional annotation showed that the predicted genes of PLA1006 were mainly associated with the metabolic pathways of amino acid, carbohydrate, cofactor, and vitamin. It also included energy metabolism, membrane transport, and signal transduction pathways. A total of three gene islands and four predicted gene clusters of CRISPR sequence in the whole genome were detected.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of potential genes for PLA degrading enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: PLA-degrading enzymes produced by the Bacillus typically belong to either proteases [18] or esterases [9]. The degradation of PLA by B. safensis has not been reported previously. To identify PLA degrading enzymes produced by B. safensis PLA 1006, the protein sequences of PLA1006 were analyzed using the software SignalP (Version: 5.0b) [28]. A total of 299 signal peptide-containing proteins were identified through this analysis. Considering that the reported PLA-degrading enzymes of bacterial origin were predominantly α/β-hydrolases (including lipases, esterases, and proteases), seven enzyme genes with signal peptides were selected. These genes were then subjected to RT q-PCR to validate the gene transcript levels when B. safensis PLA 1006 was grown with PLA as the sole carbon source. The gene information is listed in Table S1.

The differences in the transcript levels of the above seven genes when PLA 1006 was grown on MSMP and MSMG are shown in Fig. 1b. Compared to the transcript levels of PLA 1006 grown on MSMG, the strain grown on MSMP showed a significant elevation in the expression levels of triacylglycerol lipase (TGL) and S8 family serine peptidase (S8SP). The expression levels of TGL and S8SP showed 40-fold and 18-fold up-regulation, respectively. However, the expression levels of the other five selected genes: serine hydrolase (SER), site-2 protease family protein (S2P), alpha/beta hydrolase 1 (ABH1), alpha/beta hydrolase 2 (ABH2), and pectin esterase (PEE) were not significantly raised.
These results led us to consider TGL as the key enzyme for PLA degradation in the PLA1006 strain. Thus, TGL was chosen for further work.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Gene cloning and expression of PLA degrading enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: TGL gene was amplified by PCR and ligated with PET-28a(+), and the recombinant plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) for induced expression. The harvested recombinant cells were broken by ultrasound and protein purification was performed using His-tag Protein Purification beads. The enzyme activity and protein concentration during protein purification were shown in TableS2. The results of SDS-PAGE (Fig. 2A) showed that the recombinant protein was expressed in both supernatant and precipitate after the sonication of cells. Owing to the complexity of the process of purification of proteins from precipitates, only the proteins expressed in the supernatants were purified. TGL with a molecular weight of 20 kDa was purified, which was consistent with the predicted results. Western blot analysis (Fig. 2B) showed that the target protein contained His-tag and the molecular weight matched with the results of SDS-PAGE. The molecular weight of TGL was similar to triacylglycerol lipase (19.2 kDa) derived from B. pumilus [43] and lipase (19.3 kD) from B. subtilis [44]. TGLs are the smallest lipases currently identified [45].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of temperature, pH, metal ions, and chemicals on TGL
ce:section.ce:para: As shown in Fig. 2C and D, at pH 9 and 55 °C maximum efficacy of TGL was observed. These conditions were thus considered to be optimal conditions. TGL has low enzyme activity under acidic conditions, this is in agreement with the earlier reports on lipases from B. licheniformis, Paenibacillus amylolyticus, and B. subtilis [19,46–48]. Investigation of pH stability(Fig. 2E) and temperature stability (Fig. 2F) showed that the enzyme activity of TGL decreased gradually within 24 h at pH 8.0–10.0 and temperature 45–60 °C, respectively. In the experimental pH and temperature ranges, TGL showed a better stability at pH 9.0 and 45 °C. TGL retained >20 % activity after 12 h of incubation at optimum temperature 55 °C and optimum pH 9.0.

In a similar manner to the lipase derived from P. mendocina DS 04-T, the enzyme activity of TGL was increased by sodium and potassium ions (Fig. 2G) [49]. However, the presence of Cu2+ and Fe2+ significantly inhibited the enzyme activity, which was consistent with the behavior of lipase from B. subtilis [50]. In addition to this, Mn2+, Ca2+, Zn2+, and Ni2+ also inhibited the enzyme activity. In the process of TGL production and application, exposure to these metal ions should be avoided to minimize the depletion of enzyme activity. Low concentrations of Triton X-100 were found to increase the activity of TGL (Fig. 2H). This could be attributed to Triton X-100 acting as a surfactant, increasing the contact area between TGL and PLA and consequently increasing the enzyme activity [51]. However, high concentrations of Triton X-100 exhibited a negative effect on the enzyme activity. EDTA significantly inhibited enzyme activity, indicating that the enzyme is a metalloenzyme and metal ions may play an important role in the activity of the enzyme [52]. Additionally, methanol, ethanol, β-mercaptoethanol, and glycerin also reduced the enzymatic activity of TGL.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity and kinetic parameters of TGL
ce:section.ce:para: Synthesizing substrates, such as fatty acid esters of p-NP, provide a quick way to determine catalytic preferences for fatty acid chain lengths in proteins with unknown functions [53]. Based on the results (Fig. 3a) of the hydrolytic activity of TGL to p-NP substrates with different chain lengths (C2-C18), it was found that TGL demonstrated the highest hydrolytic activity towards C2 substrates and a decreasing trend in hydrolytic activity with increasing fatty acid chain length. Some strains from Bacillus also produce lipases or esterases which selectively hydrolyze short-chain fatty acid esters. 1CE esterase [54], Type II esterase [55], and enantioselective lipase [56] secreted by B. pumilus, B. licheniformis, and B. cereus, respectively, can efficiently hydrolyze the p-NP substrates of carbon chain lengths of C2, C2, and C4. The Lineweaver-Burk plot (Fig. 3b) obtained based on the reciprocal of the reaction rate and substrate concentration showed a tendency for Km to increase and Vmax to decrease with increasing fatty acid chain length of p-NP substrate. This result further highlighted that TGL has better affinity and hydrolytic ability for short-chain fatty acid ester substrates (Table S2).

Fig. 4a shows the degradation curve of TGL on PLA films. The weights of PLA films were reduced by >5 % after incubation for 12 h with TGL resulting in an average degradation rate of about 20.5 mg·cm−2·h−1 (0.425 %·h−1). Compared to the fermentation broth of the strain B. safensis PLA 1006 [22], the degradation was significantly improved due to the lower TGL expression of B. safensis in the fermentation broth and the increased concentration of recombinant proteins after induction. The degradation rate of PLA film gradually decreased with the prolonged degradation time. It was attributed to the production of lactic acid and its oligomers in the reaction system, which in turn affected the catalytic activity of TGL. The production of lactic acid and its oligomers was verified by subsequent results of MALDI-TOF-MS. The surface of the PLA films hydrolyzed by TGL at 55 °C for 12 h displayed whitening as compared with the non-treated films (Fig. 4b). The surfaces of the untreated PLA films were smooth (Fig. 4C), whereas the surfaces of TGL-treated PLA films showed obvious cracks and pit formations, indicating that the surfaces of PLA films were degraded by TGL. WCA is inversely related to the hydrophilicity [57]. The WCA of PLA films treated with TGL decreased significantly (Fig. 4D), indicating that the treatment of TGL changed the hydrophilicity of the surfaces of the PLA films surface. After incubation of TGL with PLA emulsion at 55 °C for 12 h, the PLA emulsion became more clarified, which also further confirmed the degradation of TGL on PLA (Fig. 4E).

The degradation products of PLA films were detected by MS. The TGL-treated samples displayed two peaks at m/z 89 and 161, corresponding to lactate monomer and lactate dimer, respectively, (Fig. 4G), compared to the non-treated samples (Fig. 4F). The hydrolysis of PLA by TGL produced lactic acid monomer and dimer. However, the lactate monomer and pentamer were produced upon degradation of PLA with B. safensis PLA1006 [22]. The disappearance of dimers and the appearance of pentamers suggested an additional PLA degradation mechanism in strain PLA1006.

Table 1 illustrates the results of a comparative study of TGL with several PLA-degrading enzymes of bacterial origin. The optimum pH range of TGL and the other PLA-degrading enzymes was similar, falling in the alkaline range. The optimum temperature of TGL aligned closely with lipases from P. amylolyticus [19] and Pseudomonas mendocina [58], as well as proteases from B. licheniformis [59]. The esterases from Alcanivorax borkumensis and Rhodopseudomonas palustris exhibited higher and lower optimal temperatures, respectively, than the aforementioned enzymes [21]. TGL's molecular weight is most akin to LipA from P. amylolyticus, with a 51 % amino acid sequence similarity, indicating a certain evolutionary relationship between TGL and LipA. In our study, the PLA degradation rate by TGL was 0.425 %·h−1, which surpassed that of PLA-degrading enzymes from P. mendocina and B. licheniformis but fell short compared to enzymes from A. borkumensis and R. palustris. Notably, the TGL results were obtained at much lower enzyme concentrations. Enzymatic hydrolysis of PLA can be affected not only by the catalytic efficiency of the enzyme molecule itself but also by the molecular weight and crystallinity of PLA as well as the catalytic system [21].

Sequence alignment using the END script server revealed a high degree of similarity in the amino acid sequences of triacylglycerol lipases secreted by B. pumilus (WP_105928362.1), B. licheniformis (OLQ46090.1), and B. subtilis (BAI84354.2) to that of TGL, with sequence identities of 93 %, 84 %, and 81 %, respectively. (Fig. 5 ). There are five α-helices, six β-folds, and four β-turns in the secondary structure of TGL [40]. The crystal structures of the PLA degrading enzyme secreted by Bacillus have been analyzed and they all have a common folding pattern known as α/β-hydrolase folding. Several similar triacylglycerol lipases from Bacillus, including B.pumilus B. licheniformis, and B. subtilis, contain a special conserved pentapeptide sequence Ala-X-Ser-X-Gly, different from the canonical lipase sequence motif Gly-X-Ser-X-Gly. This replacement has only been found so far in lipolytic enzymes from Bacillus species [48]. The pentapeptide sequence Ala-X-Ser-X-Gly might be a common feature of Bacillus lipases [60], and these hydrolases appear to represent a special group of enzymes in Bacillus [48].

Comprehensive analysis of XP docking and MM-GBSA results (Table S3) showed that the docking score of the lactic acid dimer with TGL was −4.415, while that of MM-GBSA was −39.50 kcal/mol. The low binding free energy and lower docking score indicated that the lactic acid dimer exhibited stability in binding to TGL. Protein structure modeling showed that the active sites of TGL were Ser77, Asp133, and His156. Lactic acid dimer got attached to the surface of the active pocket forming hydrophobic interactions with Ile135, Val136, Ala105, Leu108, and Ile12. A hydrogen bond was formed with Ser77, Met78, Ile12, and His156, while another hydrogen bond and a salt bridge were formed with Asp133 (Fig. 6 ). Biodegradation of high molecular weight PLA was slower, and hydrolysis treatment to reduce its molecular weight could improve the biodegradation efficiency of PLA [61]. This could be attributed to the spatial site resistance caused by the amino acid side chains near the catalytic center and the bulky binding conformation of high molecular weight PLA [62].

TGLs are the smallest lipases currently identified [45], TGL and all of the lipases from Bacillus have 181 amino acids [63]. TGL belongs to the α/β-hydrolase superfamily (ABH), a serine-type lipase that uses water to catalyze covalent bond cleavage. The partial amino acid sequences of ABH are conserved, mainly reflected in the amino acid sites of the catalytic triad (Ser77, Asp133, and His156), substrate-binding, and oxygen anion cavity. These amino acid sites are necessary for TGL in hydrolyzing the lipase substrates and PLA, and mutations at those sites result in a complete loss of lipase hydrolysis activity [19].

TGL derives its name from its proficiency in hydrolyzing ester bonds within triacylglycerol. In contrast, PLA is a polymer comprising lactic acid connected by ester bonds, a structural feature shared with triacylglycerol. This structural similarity raises the possibility that TGL could potentially degrade PLA by hydrolyzing the ester bonds within the PLA molecule. It's important to note that the prerequisite for TGL to catalyze hydrolysis is its stable binding to the substrate molecules. The molecular docking results affirmed this stability, indicating that amino acid residues in TGL and the lactic acid dimer could form hydrogen bonds and salt bridges, suggesting a stable binding between the two. This stable binding is essential for the effective degradation of PLA by TGL.

In this study, a triacylglycerol lipase (TGL) with the ability to degrade PLA was purified from B. safensis PLA1006. TGL contains the classical catalytic triad structure of lipase (Ser77, Asp133, and His156) and Ala-X-Ser-X-Gly sequence. The amino acid sequence is highly similar to triacylglycerol lipases from Bacillus. TGL was found to demonstrate the ability to degrade both PLA film and PLA emulsion, and the degradation products were lactic acid monomers and dimers. The wild-type TGL obtained in this work has the potential to be enhanced in its ability to catalyze PLA degradation. Further rational evolution and molecular modifications can be carried out to improve the thermal stability and catalytic activity of TGL to meet the needs of large-scale applications, and related work is in progress in our laboratory.
